passage: Dear Margit, we are home at last from the coast and I owe you the full account. The cottage you recommended was everything you promised, though the walk down to the cove has grown steeper in my memory of it, or I have grown older, and I suspect both. We had nine days of weather out of fourteen, which the landlord assured us was a triumph for June. Tomas fished every morning from the rocks below the coastguard cottages and caught exactly one mackerel the entire fortnight, which he insisted on grilling with such ceremony that the children have now told the story to everyone in the village as though he had landed a whale. Your tip about the bakery in the harbor lane saved us; we went daily, and the woman there, once she learned we knew you, would not let us pay for the almond twists on our last morning. The only disappointment was the boat trip to the seal island, cancelled twice for swell and finally taken on a gray Tuesday when the seals, every last one, had decided to be elsewhere. The children have already voted to return next year. Come with us, and bring Henrik; the cottage sleeps eight and we were only five. With love, Annelie.
question: How many mackerel did Tomas catch during the fortnight?

passage: Dear Uncle Bram, thank you for the loan of the wood chisels, which I am returning with this letter, sharpened, though probably not to your standard. The bookshelf is finished and standing in the hall, and I will defend its lean of two degrees as character. I followed your advice about cutting the housing joints by hand rather than hiring a router, and you were right that I would learn more from the first bad joint than from a whole shelf of clean machine cuts; the second joint went better, and by the fifth I stopped holding my breath. The oak came from the salvage yard on Piper Street you told me about, boards from an old chapel floor, the man said, and full of nails he had not mentioned, which cost me one chisel edge and taught me the metal detector habit permanently. Total damage: 60 dollars for the wood, one bruised thumb, and my Saturday afternoons for six weeks, which is cheaper than the 400 dollars the shop on Kerner Road wanted for their sad veneered thing. Mother says you are to come for dinner when the weather turns, and that you are not to bring anything, which you know she does not mean. Your nephew, Casper.
question: Where did the oak boards come from?
answer: the salvage yard on Piper Street

passage: My dear Rosa, your grandmother's soup recipe, since you ask so nicely, though I warn you it is less a recipe than a set of opinions. She used two hands of white beans, which in my measuring cups comes to a pound and a half, soaked overnight, and she threw the soaking water to the roses, claiming they liked it; the roses never confirmed this. The ham bone matters more than the ham: ask the butcher on Thursday, when he cuts, and take whatever he grins about. Onion, always three, never two, because her mother said two onions argue and three agree, and carrots only if the week had been good. She simmered the beans two hours before the bone went in at all, which every printed recipe reverses, and she was right and they are wrong; the beans drink the broth otherwise and turn to flannel. Salt at the end, a swallow of vinegar off the heat, and the parsley chopped so fine your knuckles ache. She fed eleven people from that pot on washing days. I have halved and halved it and it still overflows this house. Make it once as written before you improve it; that courtesy is owed to the dead. All my love to Daniel and the baby. Nonna Lucia.
question: How many onions does the soup always take?

passage: Dear Mr. Havelock, I write to thank you, at a distance of forty years, which is a delay even my mother would have called excessive. In the autumn term of my second year you kept me back after the geometry lesson, not to scold me, though I had earned it, but to hand me a battered blue book of puzzles and say only, bring it back when you have an argument with it. I had the argument. I have been having it ever since, through a degree, a doctorate, and a career spent teaching mathematics at the college in Brandt's Ferry, where I have just retired after 31 years. At the small ceremony they gave me, a colleague asked when I had decided on mathematics, and I heard myself describe your classroom, the chalk trough, the broken globe, the blue book, before I had decided to say anything at all. I tracked you through the school's old registers and your niece, who kindly supplied this address and warned me you would claim to remember nothing. Claim what you like; I remember. The book, I confess, I still have. If you will allow it, I would rather drive up and return it in person than trust the post. With respect and affection, Edwin Sorel.
question: For how many years did the writer teach at the college in Brandt's Ferry?

passage: Dearest Willa, the house is sold, and I write sitting on the last chair, which the buyers have kindly agreed to let travel with me on Thursday. Forty-two years in one kitchen, and it comes down to nineteen boxes, of which eleven are books, so you may tell your husband his theory of my character is confirmed. The garden was the hard goodbye. Your father's plum tree gave its best year ever, as though it knew, and I have put up fourteen jars, of which four ride with me to the flat and one is set aside for you, the one with the ribbon, packed where I can find it. The new people are young and asked good questions about the boiler and none about the roses, so I have written the roses a letter of instruction and taped it inside the shed door, which they will find in April and think me mad, and by June they will be grateful. The flat has a balcony that takes two chairs and, the agent swears, the evening sun. You are not to worry. Grief and relief are sharing the sofa tonight and getting along better than expected. Come for the first Sunday after the fifteenth and bring nothing but the children. Your loving mother.
question: How many jars of plums did the writer put up?

passage: Dear Fenn, a warning and an apology together: the canoe is yours for the last two weeks of August as promised, but she has developed opinions since you borrowed her last. The new seat I fitted in spring sits an inch higher than the old, which improves your back and worsens her temper in a crosswind, so kneel when it blows, as we always said and neither of us did. The slow leak is fixed, or rather moved; she now takes perhaps a cup an hour through the stern seam instead of the bow, and the bailing sponge lives under the stern thwart in a mesh bag, next to the spare line. I have left the good paddle, the cherry one your father made, hanging in the boathouse for you, on the condition, and I am serious beneath the joking, that it never touches gravel; use the plastic loaner for landings and poling, that is what the ugly thing is for. The portage wheels lost a cotter pin at Duck Narrows in July and I replaced it with wire, which holds but check it. Lake permits are in the tin with the matches. Leave me the cabin log honest and the woodpile no worse. Yours in trust, Aldo.
question: Where does the bailing sponge live?
distractors: in the tin with the matches

passage: Dear Professor Imani, you asked the seminar to write to you in five years and report honestly, and mine falls due this week. The honest report: I did not become an architect. I lasted two years at the firm in Coleharbor, drawing stairwells for buildings I never saw finished, and then, by a route involving a broken elevator, a talkative building inspector, and a summer course I took half in spite, I became a structural surveyor of old buildings, and I am happy in a way I did not know to want. I spend my days in church towers and mill basements with a torch and a notebook, deciding what is holding what, and it turns out that is the question I always cared about; your course on why buildings stand up was the only one I never skipped. Last month I certified the reopening of a 1840s rope walk that three developers had called past saving, and when the owner asked whether I was sure, I heard your voice about the difference between a crack that is moving and a crack that has finished moving, and I was sure. You may count this letter, per your old joke, as one building still standing. With gratitude, Sela Brandt.
question: What did the writer become instead of an architect?

passage: Dear Cousin Petra, the results of the great hen experiment, one year in, as promised at Christmas when you called us mad. We began in March with six hens, the black one having been added in June after what the children call the hawk day, of which we do not speak at dinner. Total eggs for the year: 1,204, which I record in the seed diary like a proper farmer and which works out near two hundred per hen, the black one excused on grounds of trauma and seniority. Costs, since your husband will ask: 340 dollars all told for feed, grit, and the electric netting, against which I set the eggs at market price and a neighborly trade with the Kohler place, tomatoes for eggs all summer, that no ledger can price fairly. The coop your Anders drew for us on the napkin held off the fox twice that we know of, tracks in the snow both mornings, and I have posted him a photograph of the scratches on the door frame as a testimonial. What nobody warns you: hens follow you like small opinionated dogs, and Marta has named them all, so soup is out of the question forever. Come in May and the orchard will be in bloom. Your cousin, Ilse.
question: How many eggs did the hens lay in the year?

passage: Dear Mr. Quayle, I write concerning the violin you sold my son at your shop on the 9th, and I ask you to read to the end before reaching for the receipt book, because this is not the letter you are expecting. The violin buzzed on the A string within a week, as you warned us it might in a house with radiators, and we brought it back Tuesday while you were at lunch. Your apprentice, a young woman whose name I did not catch, took it into the back for twenty minutes, returned it cured, and then spent a full hour with my boy, unasked and unpaid, correcting the way he had been taught to hold the bow, with a patience I have not seen from his actual teacher in two years of lessons at 40 dollars the half hour. She told him the buzz had been a loose seam, nothing he had done, which mattered to him more than she can have known, and sent him off with a practice trick involving a pencil that he has done every day since without being told. I do not want a refund. I want her name, so that when she takes students, we are first in the queue, and I want her employer to know what he has. Sincerely, Roland Vasek.
question: What did the apprentice say had caused the buzz?

passage: My dear Tobias, I have reached the age at which one distributes things, and this parcel is the start of it, so no protests. The wristwatch was my father's, bought in 1948 from his first full wage packet at the foundry, and it has been serviced faithfully every five years, most recently in March by the little shop behind the station, ask for Mr. Odum, whose ticket is in the box. It loses forty seconds a week, which my father called its opinion of the modern pace, and you are not to have that corrected. The watch goes to you and not to your brother for a reason you may as well know: when you were nine, you sat with me the whole afternoon of your grandmother's funeral winding it and asking how the escapement knew when to let go, and Anton, whom I love equally and differently, asked what it was worth. Neither answer was wrong. But a watch should live with the question it suits. Wear it to your interview next month; a watch that survived the foundry will not be frightened of a law firm. Write and tell me how it goes, and wind it in the morning, never at night. Your grandfather, Emil.
question: How much time does the watch lose each week?
